title: The Growing Lag

scenario.situation: The Kafka consumer group processing inbound telemetry events has accumulated 2–3 million messages of lag every peak window for the past two weeks, triggering on-call alerts and SLA warnings.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team lead is convinced the Kafka broker cluster is undersized and wants to provision two additional broker nodes before next week's peak.
scenario.question: Is the broker actually the bottleneck, or is something else throttling the consumer?

decisions.prompt: The team lead wants broker nodes ordered today. How do you frame your investigation before any money is spent?

options.label: Benchmark broker throughput under peak load
options.detail: Spin up a load test against the brokers and measure max throughput to confirm they are saturated.
options.consequence: The brokers handle the load test fine — they aren't saturated. But because you started from the broker hypothesis, you have no view of what is actually slow. You've spent two days confirming a negative.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's assumption and wasted time proving a non-problem.

options.label: Diagnostic pipeline decomposition
options.detail: Break the end-to-end pipeline into stages — broker, consumer, and sink — and measure latency and throughput independently at each boundary.
options.consequence: You immediately see broker network I/O is calm and consumer poll rates are healthy, but the sink write latency is spiking during the same windows the lag grows. The bottleneck is now a specific, testable stage.

options.label: Check broker disk and CPU dashboards
options.detail: Pull broker-level infrastructure metrics and look for resource saturation signals.
options.consequence: Disk and CPU look fine at peak. Nothing conclusively rules brokers in or out, and you still have no idea where in the pipeline lag is generated.
options.divergenceCost: Stayed inside the broker frame and missed the sink stage entirely.

options.label: Increase consumer group instances immediately
options.detail: Scale the consumer group horizontally now and see if lag clears.
options.consequence: Each additional consumer hits the same slow synchronous sink. Lag distributes across more consumers but does not shrink — and you now have more competing writers hammering the sink.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to a remediation before diagnosing, compounding the real problem.

decisions.prompt: Pipeline decomposition flags the sink as a suspect. Which metric do you use to confirm the bottleneck?

artifact.title: Average processing time per stage — peak window (ms)
artifact.caption: Raw average latencies. The sink bar is tall — but averages can hide whether this is a rate issue or a volume issue.

options.label: Average sink write latency (ms)
options.detail: Use the mean write duration across all sink calls during the peak window.
options.consequence: The average looks elevated but not catastrophic. At low traffic it is similar. You can't tell whether the sink is the constraint or just reflecting normal variance — the average obscures the cumulative back-pressure effect.
options.divergenceCost: Used an average that hid the back-pressure signal — a classic metric aggregation trap.

options.label: Sink write throughput vs. consumer poll rate (records/sec, normalized)
options.detail: Compare the rate at which the consumer polls records against the rate at which the sink successfully commits them, normalized to the same time window.
options.consequence: The gap is unmistakable: the consumer polls 12,000 records/sec at peak but the sink commits only 1,100 records/sec — a 10× mismatch driven entirely by synchronous per-record inserts. The broker's produce rate is unaffected throughout.

artifact.title: Throughput rate by pipeline stage — peak window (records/sec)
artifact.caption: Normalized to the same window, the sink commit rate is ~10× slower than every upstream stage. The broker is not the constraint.

decisions.prompt: The sink commit rate is 10× slower than the consumer poll rate during peak. What do you tell the team lead?

options.label: "The broker is fine — it's the synchronous sink writes. Switch to batched inserts and add partitions, problem solved."
options.detail: Make the full causal call and prescribe the fix.
options.consequence: You're likely right about the sink, but you've made a definitive causal claim from profiling data alone. If the sink slowness is itself caused by a downstream DB lock or network issue that recurs, batching may only mask it temporarily.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation without a controlled validation step.

options.label: "The throughput data points strongly to the sink, not the broker — batching writes and adding partitions is the hypothesis to test. Let's validate with a controlled off-peak trial before committing to either fix or new broker nodes."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the mechanism, and recommend a confirmatory trial.
options.consequence: The team lead gets a clear reframing backed by data, a concrete next step, and an honest scope boundary. The controlled trial confirms batching raises sink throughput to 11,200 records/sec and lag stays flat at peak — and no broker nodes are purchased.

insight: The broker was never the bottleneck — synchronous per-record inserts into the downstream sink created a 10× throughput gap that back-pressured the entire consumer group. The team's instinct to scale brokers was plausible but untested; a pipeline decomposition and a normalized throughput comparison exposed the real constraint in hours. The lesson is that Kafka consumer lag is almost always a consumer-side or sink-side problem first: check write throughput and partition parallelism before touching the broker.
